amendments.rule: Where English fuses several morphemes into one word, such as *wherein*, they share a unit. Reserve `added` for English that no morpheme licenses at all. This governs a fixed multi-word Hebrew expression the ASV renders with one English word too — `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles*, `אִם לֹא` → *surely*: the whole expression is one unit, headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme, rather than one rendered morpheme beside others marked `unrepresented`. The one-English-word condition is load-bearing in both directions: `בְּיַד` → *by* and `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* fuse, but where the ASV spends a second English word on the expression — `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses while the same idiom as *say ... nay* does not — the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. **Read that condition as one English rendering, not one English token.** A compound English preposition written in two or three words — *because of*, *by reason of*, *out of* — is a single rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and it fuses; so does an expression whose unit additionally carries a copula or other word the construction hands to the whole of it under another rule, as `לִפְנֵי` → *was before*. What defeats the condition is English the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so that each morpheme has a rendering of its own: `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives *to* to the preposition and *meet* to `פָּנֶה`, and `עַד לְ` → *until there was* gives *until* to `עַד` and the predicate's supplied copula to the `לְ` under rule 49, while the same `עַד לְ` → *to* fuses. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the second English word and ask whether a particular morpheme has lost its rendering or only the expression as a whole is diminished. What the second morpheme is tagged does not matter; a preposition before a construct noun fuses on the same terms as a compound preposition. Contiguity is part of the condition for such an expression: a verb and the preposition it governs, held apart by the subject or the object, is not one. It is not a condition on fusion generally — rule 35's *Nor* and *never* fuse across intervening material, because there the one English word still carries every morpheme's sense. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* and `הוֹסִיף ... אֶל` → *exceed* are a verb whose preposition the ASV's comparative recasting leaves unrendered, so rule 2 splits them and the preposition is `unrepresented`. Rule 22 governs a repetition of the *same* element, not the parts of an idiom.
amendments.why: Rule 30 states its condition as one English word and then offers מִפְּנֵי -> because of, which is two, as a fusion. 1CH.12 met that gap three times and had to draw the line itself: 12.1 fused מִפְּנֵי -> because of, 12.17 split לִפְנֵי -> to meet, 12.16 fused עַד לְ -> to, and 12.22 split the same עַד לְ -> until there was. Read as written, those look like one construction analysed two ways; read as one rendering rather than one token, they are one test applied four times. The corpus agrees on both halves: it fuses because of (6 units), by reason of (2, headed on reason), לִפְנֵי -> before (75) and לִפְנֵי -> was before and were before (6 units carrying a supplied copula inside the fused unit), and it splits nothing where the two morphemes share a single preposition word. The amendment adds the criterion and the subtraction test that decides it, and leaves the rest of rule 30 — the fixed-expression clause, the tagging clause, the contiguity clause, the גָּדַל ... מִן exclusion and the rule 22 boundary — exactly as it stood.

conventions: The muster idiom עֹרְכֵי / לַעֲרֹךְ מִלְחָמָה -> that could set the battle in array is divided the same way throughout the chapter (12.33, 12.35, 12.36, and 12.38 with עֹדְרֵי -> that could order): the verb takes the supplied relative and modal and the English idiom's in array, its unit discontinuous around the object under rule 25, while the object noun takes the battle with a supplied the. Where the Hebrew has no object noun at all — 12.33's לַעֲדֹר — the ASV's italicised the battle array is added, since no morpheme's rendering it completes.

The muster idiom יוֹצְאֵי צָבָא -> such as were able to go out in the host (12.33, 12.36) is divided so that the whole supplied antecedent phrase such as were able to joins the participle under rule 46, headed on the lexeme go, with out as the verb's particle under rule 44, while צָבָא takes in the host with its supplied the. The ASV writes in rather than of for this chain's relation, which the rectum takes by rule 19.

The directive he (Sd) takes the English preposition the ASV writes for the goal, and the place noun keeps its own word with any supplied the: חֶבְרוֹנָה -> to Hebron (12.23, 12.38) puts to on the directive he, and מִדְבָּרָה -> in the wilderness (12.8) puts in on it. The competing reading, which marks the morpheme unrepresented and hands the preposition to the noun, is recorded on 12.8 and was not taken anywhere in this chapter.

report: Read all 60 candidate groups and the whole dump end to end, the latter because the table is keyed by source lemma and so cannot see the six `added` units. No construction in this chapter is analysed two ways with nothing in the source licensing the difference. The one patch below changes a note, not an edge.

Near-miss 1: 12.1 מִפְּנֵי -> because of is one fused unit while 12.17 לִפְנֵי -> to meet is split. Licensed, and the reason is this chapter's one general finding: nothing in because of answers to פָּנֶה in particular, whereas meet is what פָּנֶה says. Rule 30's wording — one English word, illustrated by a two-word example — is what makes this look like a split, so the amendment fixes the wording rather than the alignments.

Near-miss 2: עַד לְ fuses to a single to in 12.16 and splits into until (עַד) plus the predicate's supplied existential there was (לְ, rule 49) in 12.22. Same test as above: in 12.22 each morpheme has English of its own. Both verses already carry review notes saying so.

Near-miss 3, the substantival article: 12.14 gives הַקָּטָן the pronoun-plus-relative he that (rule 41) and הַגָּדוֹל a bare the (rule 15), because that is what the ASV writes for each; 12.1, 12.23 and 12.40 all take rule 41, where the ASV writes a pronoun. Near-miss 4, rule 31's subtraction: the head lands on band in גְּדוּד -> band of rovers (12.21) but on figs in דְּבֵלִים -> cakes of figs (12.40). The test genuinely lands differently — band alone is a band, a דְּבֵלָה is not any cake — and 12.40's note records the tie.

The six added units agree with each other and with the morphemes beside them: 12.2's and stands at a junction with no waw (rule 42 places both waws elsewhere), 12.17 and 12.18 are supplied lexical verbs under rule 20, 12.27 a supplied noun phrase, 12.33 a supplied object and a supplied and. 12.33 marks the battle array added while 12.38 aligns the same English to מַעֲרָכָה: 12.33's Hebrew has no object noun and 12.38's does, so that is a source difference and not a split.

Rule 42 checked across the roster: 12.2 (three ands against two waws, one added), 12.24, 12.25, 12.26, 12.27, 12.28, 12.30, 12.34, 12.35, 12.37 all pair the ASV's and with the waw standing between the same two numerals. Rule 29 checked across every construct chain: fronting in 12.3 and 12.26, a supplied the where the rectum is anarthrous elsewhere, and rule 47's test applied in 12.15 (in the first month) with the correction already recorded there.

BSB: none of the 15 disagreements is a genuine error. Td x 4 and R x 6 are recastings that leave the morpheme nothing (rules 29, 40), אֶת x 3 is rule 16's ordinary ruling, and the 12.8 waw is the ASV's relative recasting. The only one with substance is עֵת at WLC.1CH.12.22.003: rule 30 would fuse לְעֶת -> from if that were the whole expression, but the Hebrew constituent is לְעֶת יוֹם and the ASV spends from day on it, so the condition is unmet and the construct keeps nothing. The edge stands; the patch corrects only its note, which cited rule 22 (repetition), a rule that does not govern here.

Three conventions recorded. The validation report's 70 repeating notes are overwhelmingly boilerplate labels (Conjunction., Proper name., Article rendered the.) rather than judgments, so recording them would hide the three that are: the two roster idioms and the directive he. The directive he might generalise beyond this chapter, but the corpus tables supplied here cover no Sd unit outside a one-word fusion, so I recorded it as a convention rather than promoting it, and did not spend the evidence round on it because it would change no alignment in 1CH.12.
